anatomy.title: Overview
anatomy.body: A flat triangular bone linking the upper limb to the axial skeleton through the clavicle. Its lateral angle forms the glenoid fossa.
bullets: Borders: superior, medial and lateral
Processes: spine, acromion and coracoid
Articulations: clavicle and humeral head

function.title: Mechanical role
function.body: Provides a mobile platform for glenohumeral motion and a broad attachment surface for stabilising muscles.
bullets: Upward rotation supports arm elevation
Retraction and protraction position the glenoid
Scapulothoracic motion contributes to shoulder rhythm

ct.title: CT appearance
ct.body: Cortical margins are high attenuation with a cancellous medullary centre. Multiplanar review is useful for the glenoid, acromion and fracture planes.
ct.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

mri.title: MRI appearance
mri.body: Marrow signal varies with sequence and age; the cortical shell remains low signal. Review the glenoid labral interface and muscle attachments.
mri.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

xray.title: Scapula · X-ray orientation
xray.body: Locate the glenoid, coracoid and scapular spine on the assembled model. AP imaging in the scapular plane and an axillary view show the glenoid–humeral relationship from different directions; a lateral scapular view adds another bony profile.
bullets: Compare the glenoid with the humeral head before isolating the scapula. Separation is a study aid and changes their apparent relationship.
A free-orbit camera is not a prescribed radiographic projection. This surface does not establish a measured joint space or normal alignment.
xray.note: Original orientation draft · independent radiology and anatomy review pending. References open separately; no images are copied or loaded, no acquisition protocol is simulated, and no patient assessment is provided.

ultrasound.title: Ultrasound window
ultrasound.body: Only accessible cortical surfaces are seen as a bright line with posterior acoustic shadow. Ultrasound is not the primary modality for the whole scapula.
ultrasound.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

pathology.title: Common patterns
pathology.body: Trauma may involve the body, neck, glenoid or processes. Morphology of the acromion and glenoid can alter shoulder mechanics.
bullets: Scapular fractures
Glenoid rim injury
Os acromiale and degenerative change

clinical.title: Clinical relevance
clinical.body: Scapular position and control are assessed alongside cuff strength and glenohumeral range.
bullets: Look for winging
Compare resting position side-to-side
Correlate focal tenderness with trauma history

quiz.title: Quick check
quiz.body: Which part of the scapula articulates with the humeral head?
bullets: Glenoid fossa
Coracoid process
Inferior angle
quiz.explanation: The humeral head meets the glenoid fossa at the glenohumeral joint.

pathology.title: Right serratus anterior · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Long thoracic nerve injury can weaken serratus anterior, allowing the medial scapular border to lift away from the chest wall.
bullets: This is a nerve-related loss of muscle control, not necessarily a tear of the muscle.
Altered scapular movement also has muscular, bony and joint-related causes; winging alone does not identify the cause.
The long thoracic nerve and dynamic scapular winging are not rendered by this muscle surface.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

clinical.title: Right serratus anterior · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Relate scapular support to overhead reach and observe the shoulder blade as well as the glenohumeral joint.
bullets: Clinical assessment compares scapular position and movement with the other side.
When nerve injury is suspected, examination and electrodiagnostic testing may help; a static model cannot establish nerve function.
The long thoracic nerve and dynamic scapular winging are not rendered by this muscle surface.
clinical.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

pathology.title: Right anconeus · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Traumatic anconeus contusion has been reported as an unusual cause of lateral elbow pain.
bullets: The published example also had other elbow injuries; it does not establish that anconeus is the usual source of lateral pain.
Anconeus epitrochlearis is a different, accessory muscle that can be associated with ulnar nerve compression. Its presence is not necessarily symptomatic.
This is the normal posterolateral anconeus, not an accessory anconeus epitrochlearis at the medial elbow.

anatomy.title: Overview
anatomy.body: Arises from the infraspinous fossa and inserts on the middle facet of the greater tuberosity.
bullets: Innervation: suprascapular nerve
Deep to posterior deltoid
Blends with the posterior cuff capsule

function.title: Action
function.body: Externally rotates the humerus and helps stabilise the glenohumeral joint.

ct.title: CT appearance
ct.body: Assess bulk, fatty replacement and osseous attachment sites.
ct.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

mri.title: MRI appearance
mri.body: Evaluate tendon continuity, muscle oedema and fatty atrophy.
mri.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

xray.title: Right infraspinatus muscle · X-ray orientation · draft
xray.body: Find infraspinatus below the scapular spine, running from its fossa toward the greater tubercle’s middle facet.
bullets: The middle facet distinguishes it from the adjacent superior and inferior cuff attachments.
Radiographs show bony orientation, not the cuff tendons or their attachment continuity. A normal X-ray does not rule out a cuff tear; MRI or ultrasound can assess soft tissues.
Keep bones visible and return model separation to zero. The assembled 3D view is an anatomy aid; rotating it does not create a radiographic projection or reveal a tendon footprint.
xray.note: Revision-bound radiologist review pending. No acquired study, patient-to-atlas registration or diagnosis is supplied. Atlas, imaging-case and lecture access remain independent.

ultrasound.title: Ultrasound appearance
ultrasound.body: Posterior scanning demonstrates the tendon inserting behind supraspinatus.
ultrasound.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

pathology.title: Common patterns
pathology.body: Tears, tendinopathy and denervation can produce weakness of external rotation.

clinical.title: Clinical relevance
clinical.body: Resisted external rotation and lag tests contribute to assessment.

quiz.title: Quick check
quiz.body: What is the principal action of infraspinatus?

anatomy.body: This narrow cuff muscle lies along the lateral scapula, below infraspinatus and above teres major.
bullets: Scapular origin near the lateral border

Axillary nerve supply (C5–C6)

function.title: Action

ultrasound.title: Right circumflex scapular artery · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: The circumflex scapular artery belongs to the scapular arterial pathway and can be discussed separately from its cutaneous perforators. An original cadaver and volunteer Doppler investigation delineated the circumflex scapular axis and perforators. pathology.title: Right thoracodorsal artery · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Thoracodorsal blood supply is important to latissimus-based reconstruction. Injury to an arterial pedicle or its relevant perforators can compromise the intended tissue supply; preservation of the motor nerve addresses a different function.
bullets: A perforator carries blood through tissue; it is not a nerve branch.

ultrasound.title: Left costocervical trunk · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: A sonographic mapping study of the brachial plexus used the deep cervical artery as a landmark near the lower cervical roots and described it as arising from the costocervical artery. That observation concerns a daughter branch, not documented detection of the complete costocervical parent. The source-labelled parent trunk can orient an anatomy discussion about the subclavian and deep cervical pathways, but a branch signal must not be promoted into proof of the whole trunk or its exact junction in an individual scan.
bullets: Keep the deep cervical landmark and the costocervical parent distinct when reading an acquired image; follow the visible continuity before assigning a vessel name.
A reported relationship near C7 and C8 is an anatomical orientation, not proof that these roots or their neighbouring artery are resolved in every examination.
The static model gives no sonographic detection rate, patient-specific depth, full parent course, Doppler result or validated nerve geometry.

pathology.title: Left costocervical trunk · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Costocervical arterial bleeding can involve both the neck and chest. A published neurofibromatosis type 1 case described aneurysmal rupture with cervical haematoma and haemothorax; this is a rare illustrative report, not a general prediction for people with NF1.
bullets: Blood in the pleural space is different from a normal vessel lying near the pleura.
A single case cannot establish rupture frequency or screening policy.
Independent costocervical trunks with original cross-region membership. Deep cervical and superior intercostal branches are not reconstructed by this selection.

ultrasound.title: Right dorsal scapular artery · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: In a healthy-volunteer ultrasound study, dorsal scapular artery detection changed with probe position in the supraclavicular region. That result illustrates the limits of one acoustic window; a vessel not seen there is not absent. Separate cadaveric work documented more than one possible origin, including transverse cervical and direct subclavian pathways. Cadaver anatomy informs variation, but it is not evidence of ultrasound performance or of the origin in a particular learner case.
bullets: On acquired images, trace a candidate artery proximally before assigning its origin; the neighbouring transverse cervical pathway can complicate a single-view identification.
Do not infer a fixed relationship to brachial plexus elements from this surface. The model does not contain validated nerve geometry or a registered sonogram.
The volunteer detection results do not establish a general screening rate, and no absent vessel, patency result or procedural target follows from one view.

ct.body: On an already acquired CT angiographic study where the vessel is opacified and the superior scapular border is covered, use serial sections and reformats to seek its course towards the notch. bullets: A published CTA case identified an aneurysmal suprascapular artery arising directly from the subclavian artery. That single abnormal case does not establish normal-artery visibility on routine CT.

ultrasound.title: Right suprascapular artery · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: At the suprascapular notch on the superior scapular border, medial to the coracoid, Doppler flow spectrum can help identify the suprascapular artery. In a healthy-volunteer study, the artery was detected in every notch that could be imaged; some notches were obscured by the clavicle.
bullets: The artery usually passes above the superior transverse scapular ligament, but vessel, ligament and nerve relationships vary.
Doppler colour alone does not establish arterial identity. A vessel unseen in one acquisition is not evidence that it is absent.

bullets: A published CTA case identified an aneurysmal suprascapular artery arising directly from the subclavian artery. That single abnormal case does not establish normal-artery visibility on routine CT.

The selected surface has no CT enhancement, measured lumen or verified patient-specific origin; an unseen segment in an acquired series is not proof of absence.

ultrasound.title: Right superior ulnar collateral artery · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: The superior ulnar collateral artery provides an orientation point where the ulnar nerve crosses the medial intermuscular septum. Ferre-Martinez and colleagues correlated ultrasound with dissection in 11 cadaveric upper limbs. Their arteries were latex-injected: the reported sonographic identification is not evidence of normal in-vivo blood flow or routine clinical detectability.
bullets: Compare a candidate vessel with the septum and neighbouring nerve on acquired images; the selected arterial mesh does not supply validated nerve geometry.
Keep superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries distinct. A nearby vascular signal alone does not establish the named branch or its full course.
No Doppler threshold, nerve-compression diagnosis or safe intervention route is inferred from this static surface.

pathology.title: Right superior ulnar collateral artery · Vascular and neurological findings are different · draft
pathology.body: In medial elbow trauma, evidence about an adjacent nerve is not a test of arterial integrity. Likewise, identifying this collateral cannot exclude a brachial injury. Vascular and neurological findings should remain separately described rather than inferred from a shared anatomical neighbourhood.
